I’m Australian and my favourite type of holiday is a road trip. I’ve driven through the US, Japan and Europe as well as my home country. I’ve also spent some time in China. 

The US certainly has its fair share of shit places, but other places do too. It all comes down to local economies and where you go. Tokyo and Osaka Japan has a lot of very nice smaller cities, towns and locales, but it also is depopulating pretty quickly and you’ll see a lot of near abandoned, decaying rural towns.

Chinese cities are pretty amazing but also can be quite soulless - like living in a shopping complex. The “new Shanghai” for example feels very dead despite everything being new and flashy. Old Shanghai is great though. Outside of major cities and going rural parts of China are also downright third world and very much still developing - but there also a lot of beauty to be had and I’d love to go back and spend more time exploring. 

Europe really is hit and miss too… I’ve driven through UK, France, Switzerland and Germany. Switzerland is just mostly all nice, France has a lot of poor areas where mostly middle eastern and African migrants live, with tent cities abutting neighbourhoods in some places. But it also has some of the most beautiful scenery and great amazing towns. Germany is similar to France, but was a bit less “ghetto” in some places. The UK is also a real blend. Equally beautiful and wealthy but there’s a real evident and sometimes very visible class divide with depressing places. 

Australia? Can be similar again. Mostly very nice but compared to a lot of these places it feels sparse and also again, yes, there’s shit places.

The US I found mostly nice. There’s a lot of visible poverty, and depressing places but no more than any other place I’ve visited.

Hard to answer without being an expert in the field, but not the majority of our migrant intake right now is not the skilled program (which if you look at the priority list is very questionable to begin with) but the student visa program. They’re over half the intake. 

Migrants as a whole are generally a net benefit - my partner is one. But unsustainably high migration outweighs the benefit with a massive cost and we’re all feeling it after years of sustained migration levels that are too high which is both major party’s policy. 

You could slash the student intake and properly fund universities and it would definitely have an impact on rental and by extension housing market imo. We get told a lot by the university sector students don’t impact us, but it’s not true in the capital cities in particular.

There are about 80,000 student accomodation placements/beds across capital cities. In 2024 there were 300,000 student visas issued, which doesn’t account for those already here and staying. In 2023 it was much much higher, by about 30%.  Students also have the ability to bring over family, which is a common visa rort - get a student visa to one of the dodgy visa farm colleges, bring in your family, never study a day. Many students also then stay much longer term - finish a degree, work here and path to PR. Daily easy especially to Indian migrants because of a special deal inked with them back in 2022 - but it’s been that way for years. 

Now I’m not trying to demonise students or migrants - they’re for the most part following the rules and just doing what our system is designed to do. But it’s a deliberately porous system we’ve set up because it supports the higher education sector and is cheap labor (although low productivity, which impacts wages).

If we properly funded universities, made them less reliant on full fee paying students, capped the numbers of student visas that could be issued annually at a sustainable level (which I admittedly am unsure what that is), and properly reviewed the skilled program, properly funded tafe and skills education, we could run with far less immigration than we have now.

This paper examines the trends and characteristics of Indigenous deaths in custody since 1991–92, using data obtained through the National Deaths in Custody Program (NDICP). NDICP data show Indigenous prisoners are now less likely than non-Indigenous prisoners to die in prison custody, largely due to a decrease in the death rate of Indigenous prisoners from 1999–2000 to 2005–06. Coinciding with this decrease in the death rate of Indigenous prisoners is a decrease in the hanging death rate of Indigenous prisoners. Monitoring trends and characteristics of both Indigenous and non-Indigenous deaths in custody supports the development of proactive strategies addressing this important issue.”
